highlights: Testosterone boosts muscle, bones, energy, and sexual health in men and women.
Women have way less testosterone than men, but it’s still super important.
Low testosterone can leave you tired, moody, and with lower libido.
You need to sleep well, exercise, manage stress, eat right, and get enough vitamin D and zinc.

blocks.text: What is Testosterone?

Testosterone is commonly referred to as the “male hormone.” And indeed, it is thanks to testosterone that adolescent boys develop deep voices, grow muscles, and experience increased body hair growth. But it is important to understand that testosterone is not only found in men, but also in women. The only difference is that men have several times more of it than women, but it is vital for both sexes.
Testosterone in Man

items: Physical strength — the hormone helps [build muscle mass](https://www.biohackers.world/blog/how-to-strengthen-muscle-growth-using-biohacking-methods) and maintain bone density.
Sexual health — regulates sex drive and erection quality.
Energy and mood — low testosterone sympthoms often accompanied by fatigue and depression.
Blood formation — stimulates the production of red blood cells, ensuring normal hemoglobin levels.

blocks.text: Testosterone in Woman
Although women have significantly less of it, it plays an equally important role:

items: Libido — affects sexual desire and satisfaction.
Bones and muscles — together with estrogens, they maintain bone strength and muscle tone.
Energy — helps you feel alert and full of vitality.
Hormonal balance — serves as a “building block” for estrogen synthesis.

Symptoms of Low Testosterone

items: In men, low testosterone (hypogonadism) manifests itself as follows:
decreased libido and erectile dysfunction;
fatigue, apathy;
decreased muscle mass, increased fat deposits;
decreased bone density.2. In women, the deficiency manifests itself differently:
decreased sex drive;
fatigue, low mood;
bone fragility in postmenopausal women.

blocks.text: How to Test Testosterone Levels

A testosterone test helps to assess the hormonal balance in the body. Your body controls the levels of testosterone in your blood. Levels are usually highest in the morning and decline during the day.

Your hypothalamus and pituitary gland control the amount of testosterone your gonads (testicles or ovaries) produce and release. The hypothalamus releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which triggers your pituitary gland to release luteinizing hormone (LH). LH then travels to your gonads and stimulates the production and release of testosterone. (LH more often stimulates the production of estrogen and progesterone in the ovaries.)
As testosterone in your blood increases, it suppresses the production of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, which helps maintain normal levels of testosterone.
If any of these organs — your hypothalamus, pituitary gland, or gonads — aren’t working normally, that can cause abnormal testosterone levels.
What are the Dangers of Testosterone Imbalance?

items: In men, low testosterone levels can lead to obesity, depression, and loss of libido. Elevated testosterone in men and women can cause aggression, acne, baldness, and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease.
In women, excess testosterone causes menstrual irregularities, facial and body hair growth, and acne. Low levels can decrease libido, cause fatigue, muscle loss, and bone fragility.

What Tests Measure Testosterone Levels?
If your healthcare provider suspects you may have irregular testosterone levels, they may order one or more tests, including:

items: Total testosterone blood test (this is usually performed in the morning since testosterone levels are highest then).
Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) blood test.
Luteinizing hormone (LH) blood test.

blocks.text: How to Increase Testosterone Naturally

Testosterone levels naturally decline with age, but some measures may slow or reverse the process. They include staying active, [getting enough sleep](https://www.biohackers.world/blog/biohacking-sleep), and limiting alcohol use. Some supplements may also help. While genetics and age play a role, lifestyle factors have a strong impact on testosterone levels. Natural strategies include many methods.
Sleep Optimization
7–9 hours per night is crucial. Even one week of restricted sleep can reduce testosterone by up to 10–15%.
Stress Management
– Chronic stress raises cortisol, which directly lowers testosterone.
– [Meditation](https://www.biohackers.world/blog/biohacking-meditation), [breathing exercises](https://www.biohackers.world/blog/breathwork-biohacking), and regular relaxation reduce this effect.
Add Physical Activity
– Resistance exercise (weightlifting, bodyweight training) boosts testosterone production.
– High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is also beneficial.
Limit Alcohol and Avoid Smoking
– Heavy drinking suppresses testosterone production.
– Smoking negatively affects hormone and vascular health.
Weight Management
– Excess body fat, especially visceral fat, is linked to lower testosterone.
– [Sustainable weight loss](https://www.biohackers.world/blog/biohacking-for-weight-loss) improves hormone balance.
Regular Sun Exposure (Vitamin D Supplements)

Vitamin D is closely linked to testosterone production.A recent study found that vitamin D deficiency leads to reduced production of testosterone, which can affect male fertility. However, there are some controversial results about this association. Thus, the association between vitamin D and testosterone levels is of clinical importance.
Balanced Nutrition
– Adequate [protein](https://www.biohackers.world/blog/biohacking-and-protein) (for muscle repair) and healthy fats (olive oil, avocados, omega-3s) support hormone synthesis.
– Key micronutrients: zinc (meat, seafood, pumpkin seeds), vitamin D (sun exposure, fatty fish, supplements), magnesium (leafy greens, nuts).
Testosterone-Boosting Foods
Testosterone production depends not only on age and genetics but also on lifestyle factors, including nutrition.
Specific nutrients — especially zinc, vitamin D, healthy fats, and antioxidants — play a crucial role in regulating testosterone levels.
While no single “superfood” can instantly boost testosterone, including specific food that improves testosterone in your daily diet helps support hormonal balance and overall well-being.

items: Lean meats and poultry. Lean beef, chicken, and turkey are rich in protein and zinc. Adequate protein supports muscle mass (which is tied to healthy testosterone), while zinc directly participates in testosterone synthesis.

Fatty Fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines, tuna). Fatty fish provide omega-3 fatty acids and vitamin D. Research links vitamin D deficiency to lower testosterone, and omega-3s reduce inflammation, supporting testicular health.
Eggs. Whole eggs (including the yolk) contain cholesterol, which is the structural building block of testosterone. They also provide vitamin D and protein.

Shellfish (especially oysters). Oysters are famous for their extremely high zinc content. Even a mild zinc deficiency is associated with reduced testosterone. Shrimp and crab also provide smaller but significant amounts.
Nuts and seeds. Almonds, walnuts, and pumpkin seeds are packed with healthy fats, magnesium, and zinc. These nutrients promote hormone regulation and better blood flow.
Leafy green vegetables. Spinach, kale, and Swiss chard are excellent sources of magnesium, which has been shown to support higher testosterone levels, particularly in active men.
Fruits (pomegranate, berries, bananas)

blocks.text: – Pomegranates are rich in antioxidants, which reduce oxidative stress and may support testosterone production.
– Berries (blueberries, raspberries, strawberries) contain polyphenols that protect cells and improve circulation.
– Bananas contain bromelain, an enzyme that may assist in testosterone metabolism.

items: Olive oil and avocados. Both provide monounsaturated fats, linked to increased testosterone and improved heart health.
Ginger. Some clinical studies show that ginger supplementation may increase testosterone levels and improve sperm health in men.
Garlic and onions. Contain compounds that may stimulate luteinizing hormone (LH), which signals the testes to produce more testosterone.

blocks.text: Incorporating a variety of these foods into a [balanced diet](https://www.biohackers.world/blog/biohacking-diet) supports not just testosterone production but also overall metabolic, cardiovascular, and reproductive health. The key is diversity and balance — no single food can replace a healthy lifestyle, regular exercise, and adequate sleep.
Supplements for Testosterone

Many people may turn to [vitamins and supplements](https://www.biohackers.world/blog/best-biohacking-supplements) to boost testosterone. However, some studies have found that despite claims of such supplements boosting testosterone, only a small percentage actually do.

Many vitamins are important for optimum health and testosterone levels, such as vitamin D. Getting at least 15 minutes of direct sunshine each day can also help manage vitamin D levels. Food sources high in vitamin D include salmon and other fatty fish, as well as fortified milk and cereal products.

DHEA is a hormone that helps produce testosterone and other hormones affecting body composition. As a person ages, DHEA levels drop, as do testosterone levels. One study, a trusted source, found that DHEA supplements are effective in increasing testosterone levels. However, it varies for different groups of people.
Other most common supplements for testosterone:

items: Vitamin D
Known as the “sunshine vitamin,” vitamin D deficiency is linked to lower testosterone.
Supplementation may help raise levels, especially in people with deficiencies.
Zinc
Essential for testosterone production.
Even mild zinc deficiency can reduce testosterone. Supplementation is most effective if intake from the diet is low.
Magnesium
Plays a role in hundreds of biochemical reactions, including hormone regulation. Studies suggest that magnesium supplementation can improve testosterone levels, especially in active men.
Ashwagandha
An adaptogenic herb used in traditional medicine.
Some studies show it can increase testosterone and improve sperm quality, while also reducing stress (high cortisol can suppress testosterone).
Fenugreek
Herb rich in compounds (furostanolic saponins) that may help maintain healthy testosterone levels.
Some clinical trials suggest improvements in libido and energy.
DHEA (Dehydroepiandrosterone)
A hormone produced naturally in the adrenal glands.
Supplements may slightly increase testosterone in older adults, but results are inconsistent.
Tribulus Terrestris
A popular herbal supplement for testosterone and libido.
Evidence is mixed: it may improve sexual desire but doesn’t consistently raise testosterone in healthy men.

blocks.text: Many men and women look to dietary supplements to boost testosterone levels. While lifestyle factors (sleep, diet, exercise) play a much bigger role, certain supplements may help support hormonal health. It is important to note that results vary, and not all supplements are backed by strong clinical evidence.
To Sum Up

Testosterone development starts before birth and assists in the development of the male sex organs. It drives libido, sperm production, body fat distribution, muscle strength, and red blood cell creation in males. Women also produce testosterone in their ovaries and adrenal glands, but they produce significantly lower levels than men.

People can gain testosterone naturally through diet and [exercise](https://www.biohackers.world/blog/fitness-and-biohacking) or, in some cases, through supplementation. However, there is no evidence to prove that testosterone therapy raises testosterone in healthy males. Testosterone is so much more than its reputation would suggest. Men and women need the proper amount of testosterone to develop and function normally. However, the optimal amount of testosterone is far from clear.

Checking testosterone levels is as easy as having a blood test. The difficult part is interpreting the result. Levels vary over the course of the day. It’s best to measure free testosterone levels in the morning. Even with an abnormally low level that is replicated on a repeat test, the decision to begin testosterone replacement therapy and the proper dose requires a careful conversation with your doctor.
